# Boundary Estate

The world's first council housing estate

London is home to some of the world's most striking architecture and innovative engineering. Whether driven by divine purpose or the needs of a growing population, the grand designs of architects and engineers have shaped the identity of the city and the lives of Londoners. Here we take a look at the Boundary Estate in London, E2.

## The Boundary Estate

The Boundary Estate was the world's first council housing estate.

The Housing of the Working Classes Act, 1885 provided a number of measures through which local authorities could develop new housing stock and tackle the problem of the 'slums' (areas of low-quality accommodation, usually associated with poverty and crime).

In London, it wasn't until the formation of the London County Council (LCC) in 1889 that these new measures were utilised. One of the first areas to be reviewed by the LCC was a slum known as the Old Nichol, on the edge of Shoreditch and Bethnal Green. The area was renowned for its dreadful living conditions and extreme poverty and even gave rise to a bestselling novel 'A Child of the Jago' by Arthur Morrison in 1896.

The slum was replaced by the Boundary Street scheme, designed for the LCC by Owen Fleming. Officially opened in 1900 by the Prince of Wales, the new estate provided five storey tenement blocks and housed 5,524 people in 1,069 separate residences. The centrepiece of the estate was Arnold Circus, a raised ornamental garden. The architectural style chosen by the LCC's architects took inspiration from one of the great architects of the period, Richard Norman Shaw.

London Picture Archive - 254139 Boundary Estate at Arnold Circus, c.1907.

London Picture Archive - 253564 View of Boundary Estate with garden, 1907.

The scheme demolished 730 houses, displaced over 5000 people and even renamed Old Nichol Street in its determination to vanquish the slum, yet the residents of the Old Nichol were not rehoused in the new accommodation.

However, the Boundary Estate in its day was considered revolutionary for the facilities it provided for residents: 18 shops, a surgery, workshops, a central laundry with bathrooms, two clubrooms and sites for two schools. The tenement blocks remain along with the bandstand at Arnold Circus and are Grade II listed.

London Picture Archive - 254048 Boundary Estate: interior of laundry room, Arnold Circus in 1964.
